title: Payroll Event Processor
flaw: PayrollEvent models four mutually-exclusive event shapes as one flat interface with a `type` discriminator plus a pile of unrelated optional fields, instead of a discriminated union - so an event object can carry fields that don't belong to its type (or omit required ones) with no compile error, and toLineItem's final branch is an unconditional catch-all ('correction - and, for now, anything else') with no exhaustiveness check, so a new event type added later silently falls into the correction branch (wrong description, wrong amount) instead of failing to compile. Regenerated to replace an earlier (incorrectly generated) debugging exercise - see exercise 5's note. First appearance of the typescript-modeling category.
key_learnings: Discriminated union (base type intersected with a per-type variant) + a switch over the tag + assertNever(event) in default is the right shape - it closes both problems the README called out: invalid field combinations become unconstructable, and a forgotten branch for a new event type becomes a compile error instead of a silent default-branch fallthrough.

assertNever only forces a compile error for code the compiler actually type-checks. Adding the 'rehire' bonus type and a matching handler proved the mechanism works, but that guarantee doesn't automatically extend across any boundary the compiler doesn't see, like a hand-constructed test object, JSON.parse output, or an `as` cast.

A field marked 'required' on a union member but still backed by a `?? 0`/`?? 'Bonus'` runtime fallback isn't really required - the fallback is standing in for exactly the undefined case the required annotation was supposed to rule out.

Partial<T> over a union type only exposes the keys common to every branch (keyof of a union is the intersection of each member's keys, not the union of them), so a test seam helper typed as `Partial<PayrollEvent>` silently lost access to every type-specific field the moment the type became a discriminated union, rather than erroring loudly.

vitest (via esbuild) does not type-check test files, so a broken seam helper's test suite can pass 8/8 at the same time `tsc --noEmit` fails on the same files - confirmed directly by running both against identical code and getting opposite verdicts.
mistakes: Made every PayrollEvent field required per-branch but left the `?? 0`/`?? 'Bonus'` fallbacks in the handler functions in place 'just to pass tests,' which meant the new required-field guarantee didn't actually hold against the test file itself.

Added the `rehire` branch, its handler, and the matching switch case correctly, but didn't update the test file's seam helpers (`hireEvent`, `terminationEvent`, etc.) to match the new discriminated-union shape - they were still typed as `overrides: Partial<PayrollEvent>`, which no longer type-checked once PayrollEvent became a union, so `tsc --noEmit` failed even though `npm test` passed. Needed a second push to fix, after the first claimed fix didn't actually change the file.
Left an unused `import { assert } from "vitest"` in starter.ts; flagged but left unfixed by choice to move on.
review_changes: Confirmed the discriminated-union/assertNever/helper-extraction approach is correct and matches both goals stated in the exercise's README.

Walked through why keeping required fields alongside `?? 0` fallbacks doesn't close the gap the exercise is about, tying it to the general principle that compile-time guarantees only hold for code the compiler actually runs over, not data crossing an unchecked boundary.

Verified the bonus challenge directly: added the `rehire` type/handler/case on the `payrolleventprocessor` branch, ran `tsc --noEmit`, and confirmed assertNever's exhaustiveness check genuinely works - no error once rehire was handled.

Found and diagnosed the Partial<PayrollEvent>-over-a-union bug in the seam helpers by actually running `tsc --noEmit` against the pushed branch rather than taking the description at face value - it failed with 5 real errors while `npm test` passed cleanly, demonstrating the vitest-doesn't-type-check point concretely.
After the fix was pushed, re-ran `tsc --noEmit` and `npm test` again and confirmed the seam-helper errors were gone (8/8 tests still passing), leaving only the pre-existing unused-import nit.
next_focus: Remove the unused `assert` import from starter.ts - flagged, left open by choice.

When a type becomes a discriminated union, check any existing `Partial<T>` usages elsewhere in the codebase (test helpers, mock builders, etc.) - keyof a union only covers fields common to every branch, so Partial<Union> silently weakens instead of erroring, which is easy to miss.

Treat 'field is required, but a runtime fallback is still there to handle it being missing' as a smell worth catching early in future typescript-modeling exercises - if removing the fallback would break a test, the field isn't actually required yet.

title: Course Enrollment Engine
flaw: attemptEnrollment conflates checking enrollment eligibility (prerequisites, schedule conflict, credit hour limit, seat availability) with committing it: a successful check also decrements section.seatsAvailable, pushes onto student.schedule, and increases student.currentCreditHours as a side effect, so there's no way to safely preview eligibility (e.g. for a 'Would I get in?' course-planner tool) without also consuming a seat and enrolling the student - same query/command-separation smell as the prior (needs_revision) exercise, held at the same category and difficulty since that one's fix didn't reach the public API. Domain changed to education to avoid repeating travel/airline.
key_learnings: Correctly diagnosed that the fix needed to land on the public API: exported `canEnroll(section, student)` as a pure, side-effect-free preview, and had `attemptEnrollment` delegate to it - mutating `seatsAvailable`/`schedule`/`currentCreditHours` only once `canEnroll` returns eligible. This is exactly the gap that sent the prior Fare Upgrade Engine exercise back for revision (its split stayed module-private).
Wired the bonus audit log so it only pushes from `attemptEnrollment`'s commit path, not from `canEnroll`'s preview path - matches the bonus's 'every committed enrollment, not every check' ask.
Preserved the four eligibility rules and their original order (prerequisites, time conflict, credit limit, seat availability) while doing the split, per the restriction.
mistakes: The audit log entry is built as `{...section, id: student.id}`, which spreads the whole `Section` object (including its own `id`, e.g. 'CS201-A') and then immediately overwrites that same-named `id` key with the student's id. Confirmed by running it: the logged entry's `id` ends up as the student's id, and the section's own id is silently discarded - only `courseCode` survives, so two sections of the same course (two time slots of CS201, say) would be indistinguishable in the log. Undercuts the bonus's own stated goal ('how many students enrolled in *this section*').
review_changes: Ran the submitted branch (`courseenrollment`) against the exercise's own test suite and `tsc --noEmit`: 5/5 passing, clean compile.

Probed the exact scenario from the README's breaking point: a section with one seat left, two students both calling `canEnroll` any number of times before either commits. Confirmed `canEnroll` never touches `section.seatsAvailable` no matter who calls it or how many times, and only the real `attemptEnrollment` call consumes the seat - the second student correctly gets 'Section is full.' once the first has committed. This is the exact guarantee the prior exercise was missing.
Reproduced the audit-log push by hand to confirm the `id` field ends up as the student's id rather than the section's, confirming the courseCode-only identification gap.
next_focus: When building a logged/derived shape from two different entities that happen to share a field name (here, both `Section` and `Student` have an `id`), name the two fields distinctly in the merged shape (`sectionId`/`studentId`) instead of spreading one entity and overwriting a same-named field from the other - spread-then-override order is a silent trap.

title: Price Drop Alert Feed
flaw: PriceAlertBanner's effect cleanup calls connection.pause() instead of connection.close() when a listing is navigated away from or the banner unmounts - pause() only stops dispatch, it doesn't release the connection from priceFeed's internal tracking (that's what close() does), so every listing a shopper has ever viewed leaves behind a permanently paused-but-still-tracked connection. Nothing errors or visibly breaks in normal single-session use (the symptom - a far higher priceFeed.trackedConnectionCount() than the number of listings currently on screen - is silent unless you specifically go looking for it), but it sets up exactly the failure the README describes: a prospective 'resume after reconnect' feature that revives paused connections would resurrect price-drop alerts for cars the shopper stopped viewing long ago.
